definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Scripture, authoritative teaching: its ordinance (śāstra-vidhi) is the authority (pramāṇa) for settling what is to be done and not done; one who sets it aside and acts from desire attains neither perfection, happiness nor the highest goal (16.23–24); Arjuna asks about those who set it aside yet sacrifice with faith (17.1); terrible austerity not enjoined by it is of demonic resolve (17.5–6).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Hypocrisy, ostentation: the first mark of the demonic endowment (16.4); the demonic act and sacrifice with it (16.10, 16.17); austerity and sacrifice done for show are rājasic (17.12, 17.18), and terrible austerity joined with it is demonic (17.5).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Arrogance: a mark of the demonic endowment (16.4); resorted to, with ego, force, desire and anger, by those who hate the Lord in all bodies (16.18); cast off by one fit for becoming brahman (18.53).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Modesty, shame at wrongdoing: one of the qualities of the divine endowment (16.2).

literal: the state of one who says 'it is' (asti)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Affirming faith (saying 'it is'): one of the brāhmaṇa's actions born of his nature, with calm, restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance, uprightness, knowledge and realised knowledge (18.42).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The threefold impulse to action: knowledge, the object of knowledge and the knower (18.18).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The threefold composition of action: instrument, act and doer (18.18).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The divine endowment: twenty-six qualities from fearlessness and purity of being to absence of excessive pride (16.1–3); it leads to release, and Arjuna is born to it (16.5).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The demonic endowment: hypocrisy, arrogance, excessive pride, anger, harshness and ignorance (16.4); it leads to bondage (16.5); its bearers are portrayed at length (16.7–20) and the Lord casts them into demonic wombs (16.19).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Excessive pride, conceit: one of the six marks of the demonic endowment (16.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Faith, threefold according to one's own nature (17.2); it accords with one's being, for a person is made of faith — as his faith, so is he (17.3); sāttvic austerity is done with the highest faith (17.17); what is done without faith is 'asat' and of no worth here or hereafter (17.28); hearing the Gītā with faith brings the worlds of the meritorious (18.71).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Austerity, threefold as of body (worship of gods, twice-born, teachers and the wise; purity, uprightness, celibacy, non-harm), of speech (non-agitating, true, pleasant, beneficial speech; recitation) and of mind (serenity, gentleness, silence, self-restraint, purity of disposition) (17.14–16); sāttvic, rājasic or tāmasic (17.17–19); terrible austerity outside scripture that torments the body is demonic (17.5–6); with sacrifice and giving it is not to be given up, being a purifier of the wise (18.5).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Giving: sāttvic when given because it ought to be given, to one who makes no return, at the right place and time to a fit recipient; rājasic when given for a return or fruit or grudgingly; tāmasic when given wrongly and with contempt (17.20–22); not to be given up (18.5); generosity is a kṣatriya's action (18.43).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Sacrifice: sāttvic when offered by rule without desire for fruit, as what ought to be offered; rājasic when aimed at fruit or for show; tāmasic when without rule, food distributed, mantras, fee or faith (17.11–13); acts of sacrifice begin with 'oṃ' (17.24); not to be given up but done without attachment and fruit (18.5–6).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Food, threefold as dear to the sāttvic (increasing life, vitality, strength, health, happiness; savoury, rich, lasting), the rājasic (pungent, sour, salty, very hot, burning; bringing pain and disease) and the tāmasic (spoiled, putrid, stale, leftover, impure) (17.7–10).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: '(Oṃ) tat sat', the threefold designation of brahman by which brāhmaṇas, Vedas and sacrifices were ordained of old (17.23): rites begin with oṃ (17.24); acts are done with 'tat' without aiming at fruit by seekers of release (17.25); 'sat' is said of being, goodness, praiseworthy acts, steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity and giving, and action for that purpose (17.26–27). (This edition omits 'oṃ' in 17.23.)
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The first member of the designation of brahman '(oṃ) tat sat'; uttering it, the acts of sacrifice, giving and austerity of the expounders of brahman always begin (17.23–24).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: 'Sat' is used for being (sad-bhāva) and goodness (sādhu-bhāva), for a praiseworthy act, for steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity and giving, and for action done for that purpose (17.26–27).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: In 17.28 'asat' is what is offered, given, practised or done without faith: of no worth either after death or here — the ethical-ritual counterpart of 'sat', not ontological non-being.

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Renunciation, which the sages know as laying aside desire-prompted actions (18.2); renunciation of prescribed action is not fitting and, if from delusion, tāmasic (18.7); through renunciation one with unattached understanding reaches the supreme perfection of freedom from action (18.49); all actions are to be renounced to Kṛṣṇa 'in thought' (cetasā, 18.57).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Relinquishment: what the discerning call giving up the fruit of all actions (18.2); Kṛṣṇa's conclusion is that it is threefold (18.4) — tāmasic when prescribed action is given up from delusion, rājasic when given up as painful, sāttvic when action is done as what ought to be done without attachment and fruit (18.7–9); since the embodied cannot give up action entirely, the relinquisher (tyāgin) is the one who gives up the fruit (18.11); it is also a quality of the divine endowment (16.2).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Giving up the fruit of all actions — the definition of tyāga (18.2); the one who does it is the relinquisher (18.11); the threefold fruit of action does not come after death to such renouncers (18.12).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Actions prompted by desire; laying them aside is what the sages know as saṃnyāsa (18.2).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Prescribed action: its renunciation is not fitting (18.7); done as what ought to be done, without attachment and fruit, it is sāttvic relinquishment (18.9) and sāttvic action (18.23); action 'fixed by one's own nature' (svabhāva-niyata) incurs no fault (18.47).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The seat — first of the five causes of every action named in the Sāṃkhya (18.14).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The doer: the second of the five causes (18.14); one who sees the self alone as doer does not see (18.16); a member of the threefold composition of action (18.18) and threefold by the guṇas (18.26–28).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The instrument(s): the third of the five causes of action, 'of various kinds' (18.14), and a member of the threefold composition of action (18.18).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The divine factor, fifth of the five causes of action (18.14); the verse does not define it.

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Steadfastness: a quality of the divine endowment (16.3) and of the sāttvic doer (18.26); threefold by the guṇas — sāttvic when it holds the activities of mind, breath and senses through unwavering yoga, rājasic when it holds to dharma, pleasure and wealth desiring fruit, tāmasic when a fool will not let go of sleep, fear, grief, despondency and intoxication (18.33–35); restraining oneself with it is a step to becoming brahman (18.51).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Understanding, threefold by the guṇas: sāttvic when it knows engaging and refraining, what to do and not do, what to fear and not fear, bondage and release; rājasic when it knows dharma and adharma wrongly; tāmasic when, covered by darkness, it takes adharma for dharma (18.30–32); a purified understanding begins the discipline of 18.51; an untainted understanding marks the one who is not bound (18.17).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Happiness, threefold (18.36–39): sāttvic — like poison at first and nectar in the end, born of the serenity of the understanding of the self, delighted in through practice and ending sorrow; rājasic — from sense-contact, nectar at first and poison in the end; tāmasic — deluding the self first and last, arising from sleep, sloth and heedlessness.

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The supreme perfection of freedom from action (naiṣkarmya-siddhi), attained through renunciation by one whose understanding is unattached everywhere, who has conquered himself and is free of longing (18.49).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Having become brahman: the one fit for becoming brahman (brahma-bhūya) after the discipline of 18.51–53, who, serene, neither grieves nor desires, is the same to all beings and attains supreme devotion to the Lord (18.53–54).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Supreme devotion to Kṛṣṇa, attained by the one who has become brahman (18.54), by which he knows the Lord in truth and enters him (18.55); one who declares the secret teaching to devotees 'having done supreme devotion' comes to him (18.68).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: One's own dharma, better even when deficient than another's well performed; doing the action fixed by one's own nature one incurs no fault (18.47); the action one is born to is not to be given up even if faulty (18.48); devoted to his own action (sva-karman) a man attains perfection by worshipping with it the one from whom beings proceed (18.45–46).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Own nature: faith is born of it (17.2); the actions of the four classes are distributed by the guṇas arising from it (18.41–44); action fixed by it incurs no fault (18.47); bound by action born of it, Arjuna will do even against his will what he does not wish to do (18.60).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The four classes — brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra — whose actions are distributed by the guṇas arising from their own nature (18.41): calm, restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance, uprightness, knowledge, realised knowledge and affirming faith for the brāhmaṇa; heroism, vigour, steadfastness, skill, not fleeing in battle, generosity and lordliness for the kṣatriya; agriculture, cattle-keeping and trade for the vaiśya; service for the śūdra (18.42–44).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The Lord who dwells in the region of the heart of all beings and makes them revolve by his māyā as if mounted on a machine; he is to be taken as the sole refuge (18.61–62). The demonic say the world is without a Lord (anīśvara, 16.8) and one of them boasts 'I am lord' (16.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The power by which the Lord in the heart makes all beings revolve as if mounted on a machine (18.61).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: (1) The Lord's grace: by it one who acts while depending on him attains the eternal abode (18.56), crosses all difficulties (18.58), attains supreme peace (18.62); Arjuna regains memory by it (18.73); Sañjaya heard the dialogue by Vyāsa's grace (18.75). (2) Serenity: of mind, an austerity of mind (17.16); of the understanding, the source of sāttvic happiness (18.37).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Going for refuge to the Lord alone with one's whole being, by whose grace one attains supreme peace and the eternal abode (18.62); the 'most secret' word: relinquishing all dharmas, come to me alone for refuge; I will free you from all evils; do not grieve (18.66).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Secret: the knowledge declared is 'more secret than the secret' (18.63); the final word is the 'most secret of all' (18.64); the 'supreme secret' is to be told to devotees (18.68) and not to those without austerity, devotion, wish to hear, or who cavil (18.67); Sañjaya heard 'this supreme secret' from Kṛṣṇa (18.75).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Whoever studies the dialogue of Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna worships Kṛṣṇa with the sacrifice of knowledge (18.70).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Memory/recollection, which Arjuna says he has regained by Kṛṣṇa's grace as his delusion is destroyed (18.73); the verse does not say recollection of what.

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Delusion: the demonic take up false notions through it (16.10) and are caught in its net (16.16); giving up prescribed action from it is tāmasic (18.7), as is action undertaken from it (18.25); through it Arjuna does not wish to do what his nature will make him do (18.60); Kṛṣṇa asks whether his delusion born of ignorance is destroyed (18.72) and Arjuna answers that it is (18.73).

literal: mind; that which is conscious (as if)

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Thought: the demonic are led astray by many thoughts (aneka-citta-vibhrānta, 16.16); Arjuna is told to have his thought on Kṛṣṇa (mac-citta) constantly and so cross all difficulties by his grace (18.57–58).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Thought: those who torment the body with unscriptural austerity are without thought (acetas, 17.6); all actions are to be renounced to Kṛṣṇa in thought (cetasā, 18.57); Kṛṣṇa asks whether Arjuna heard with one-pointed thought (ekāgreṇa cetasā, 18.72).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Desire: insatiable desire drives the demonic, who hold the enjoyment of desires highest and say the world is caused by desire (16.8, 16.10–12); with anger and greed it is the threefold gate of hell (16.21); acting on its impulse, casting aside scripture, brings no perfection (16.23); cast off by one fit for becoming brahman (18.53).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Anger: a mark of the demonic endowment (16.4) and one of the three gates of hell (16.21); freedom from it (akrodha) is a divine quality (16.2).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Greed, one of the three gates of hell with desire and anger (16.21); the rājasic doer is greedy (18.27).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Hell, into which the deluded demonic fall (16.16); desire, anger and greed are its threefold gate, destructive of the self (16.21).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Ego, 'I'-making: resorted to by the demonic (16.18); joined with terrible austerity (17.5); rājasic action is done with it (18.24); the one whose state is not ego-made is not bound even in slaying (18.17); to be cast off (18.53); out of it Arjuna might refuse to listen (18.58) or resolve not to fight (18.59).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Lord of yoga: Sañjaya's name for Kṛṣṇa, from whom he heard the yoga directly (18.75) and with whom, and Arjuna, fortune and victory are found (18.78).

literal: son of Vasudeva; the indwelling god

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Name of Kṛṣṇa in Sañjaya's closing words: the dialogue of Vāsudeva and Pārtha (18.74).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Authority, means of right knowledge: scripture (śāstra) is Arjuna's authority for what is to be done and not done (16.24).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Rule, ordinance: the ordinance of scripture (śāstra-vidhi) is not to be cast aside (16.23, 17.1); the demonic sacrifice without it (16.17); sāttvic sacrifice is as seen in the rule, tāmasic sacrifice without it (17.11, 17.13).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: The three strands born of prakṛti from which no being on earth or among the gods is free (18.40); faith, food, sacrifice, austerity, giving (17.2–22), relinquishment (18.4–9), knowledge, action, doer, understanding, steadfastness and happiness (18.19–39) are each threefold by them; the actions of the four classes are distributed by the guṇas arising from their nature (18.41).

literal: that which brings forth; nature, source

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Nature: the three guṇas are born of it (18.40); Arjuna's nature will compel him to fight whatever he resolves (18.59).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Forbearance: one of the brāhmaṇa's actions born of his nature (18.42).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: (1) Engaging in action, paired with nivṛtti (refraining): the demonic know neither (16.7), the sāttvic understanding knows both (18.30). (2) The procession/activity of beings, which is from the Lord (18.46).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Refraining from action, paired with pravṛtti: the demonic do not know it (16.7); the sāttvic understanding knows it (18.30).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Complete perfection, attained by a man devoted to his own action (18.45).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Those who have renounced — contrasted with those who have not relinquished (atyāgin): the threefold fruit of action never comes to them after death (18.12).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Fearlessness, first of the qualities of the divine endowment (16.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Self-restraint: a quality of the divine endowment (16.1) and a brāhmaṇa's action (18.42).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Calm, the first of the brāhmaṇa's actions born of his nature (18.42).
Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Silence, an austerity of the mind (17.16).

Bhagavad Gītā 16–18: Cavilling: the demonic are cavillers (16.18); the teaching is not to be told to one who cavils at Kṛṣṇa (18.67); one who hears it with faith and without cavilling reaches the worlds of the meritorious (18.71).
